_note: Hand-curated from the Policy Whiplash evidence dossier (research/compass_artifact_wf-e9ff7eff, jonno.nz repo). RULES: sunk_nzd and firm[] hold ONLY individually-cited, directly sunk or cancellation/exit costs. Projections and politically-claimed totals live in contested[] and are NEVER summed. extra_costs[] is factual context, not counted. sunk_nzd: null means money was spent but no clean figure is on the public record yet; 0 means the reversal had no direct sunk cost. consequential[] holds real, individually-cited money spent BECAUSE of a reversal but that bought something (replacement programmes, re-establishment costs) — displayed separately, NEVER summed into sunk totals.

contested.label: Estimated compensation for terminating charter contracts (2018)
contested.note: A reported estimate of up to $1m per school across twelve operating and five approved schools. Actual settlements were negotiated school by school and no total was published. An estimate, never counted.

contested.label: NZEI's OIA-based cost of the 2014-18 experiment
contested.note: Union calculation: up to $48,421 per student per year, with ~30% of spend on Ministry overhead. Operational spending that bought real schooling; attributed, never counted.

contested.label: NZEI's per-student cost of the revived scheme
contested.note: Divides $37.4m of early-stage spend by 427 enrolments as at December 2025. The government counters that rolls in the original seven schools had tripled by March 2026 and that ongoing funding follows the child at state-school rates. Neither side's number is counted.

projects.summary: Opened 2014, abolished 2018, reopened 2025 — the public paid for the conversions both ways.
projects.plain: Charter schools are publicly funded schools run by private sponsors with freedom over curriculum, hours and pay. New Zealand opened its first in 2014 under a National-ACT deal, abolished the model in 2018 and converted all twelve schools into the state system, then recreated it in 2024 with $153m in funding. Within a decade the public paid to convert schools out of the model, then back into it.

events.what: National-ACT confidence and supply agreement commits to trialling charter schools in areas such as South Auckland and central/eastern Christchurch. (The agreement predates the new ministry's swearing-in on 14 December 2011.)
Education Amendment Bill passes its third reading 62 votes to 57, creating 'partnership schools | kura hourua' (Education Amendment Act 2013).
First five partnership schools open in Auckland and Northland for Term 1 2014.
Hipkins issues formal notice ending all charter contracts at the close of the 2018 school year; every operating school applies to join the state system.
Education Amendment Bill passes its third reading 63 votes to 56, removing the model from law; the twelve schools convert to designated character or state-integrated status.
National-ACT coalition agreement pledges to bring charter schools back.
Budget 2024 allocates $153m over four years for up to 15 new charter schools and 35 state-school conversions.
Education and Training Amendment Bill passes its third reading, re-establishing charter schools.
First of seven new charter schools open for Term 1 2025; the rest open by 10 February.

Three more schools announced for Term 1 2026, taking the total to 14 against Budget 2024's envelope of up to 50; the Charter School Agency is weighing four formal state-school conversion applications.
No state school has yet converted — Seymour says property liabilities are putting boards off; 16 charter schools with 1,471 students as at 1 March 2026.

projects.name: TVNZ–RNZ Merger (ANZPM)

firm.label: Final establishment-programme spend: contractors, reimbursements, overheads, boards
firm.source: Ministry for Culture and Heritage final costings, reported by RNZ (and 1News), 5 Apr 2023

projects.firm_note: MCH final costings: ~$12m on contractors and consultants (including PwC and Deloitte, averaging ~$6,000/week, with engagements dating back to January 2020 — so the total includes pre-announcement programme work), $3m reimbursing RNZ, TVNZ and NZ On Air for project work, $2.6m on offices and overheads, and ~$400k on the governance group and establishment board — including $16,000 paid to the board after cancellation. The widely-reported ~$16.1m was the interim figure at the time of scrapping; $19.6m is the final number. MCH returned the unspent $24.8m of its $44m transition budget.

extra_costs.label: Consolation funding
extra_costs.note: With the merger dead, RNZ was handed an extra $25.7m a year (and NZ On Air a boost) to 'strengthen public media' instead (1News/NZ Herald, Apr 2023). Real money, but a replacement policy — never counted here.

contested.label: Budget 2022 Crown funding earmarked for the new entity
contested.note: Allocated for ANZPM's first three years from 2023 and freed up when the merger died. A would-have-cost, not money spent. Never counted.

projects.summary: $19.6m to design a broadcaster that never went to air — scrapped by the government that announced it.
projects.plain: Labour's plan to fold TVNZ and RNZ into one new public broadcaster, Aotearoa New Zealand Public Media, due on air by mid-2023. Eleven months after the announcement, new PM Chris Hipkins scrapped it in his cost-of-living policy reset — before the entity ever legally existed. Final costings put the spend at $19.6m, roughly 60 percent of it on contractors and consultants.

events.what: Government-commissioned business case backs replacing TVNZ and RNZ with a single new public media entity.
Cabinet decision announced: TVNZ and RNZ to be folded into a new public media entity — initially as its subsidiaries — operational by 1 July 2023. Establishment board to follow within a month.
Budget 2022 earmarks $327m over three years for the new entity.
Aotearoa New Zealand Public Media Bill introduced (first reading passes 26 July); legal establishment planned for 1 March 2023.
Hipkins' policy reset stops the merger entirely — same government, eleven months after announcing it. RNZ and NZ On Air get funding boosts instead.
Final costings released: $19.6m spent, ~60% of it on contractors and consultants; board paid $16,000 after the halt.

projects.name: Mill Road Corridor
projects.firm_note: Properties were bought along the corridor by Auckland Transport and, from 2020, Waka Kotahi, and the road was planned twice — but no clean sunk-cost or property-spend figure has ever been published; the agency was tight-lipped even before the scrapping. Contributes $0 to every total here until a figure is sourced.

extra_costs.label: Property purchases
extra_costs.note: Auckland Transport began buying properties along the corridor, with Waka Kotahi taking over the purchasing from 2020. The total was never disclosed (RNZ), and the land is back in play now the corridor is revived.

extra_costs.label: Round two planning bill
extra_costs.note: $91.1m approved in April 2025 for Stage 1 design and consents alone — for a corridor first consulted on by Manukau City Council in 2009, route-protected by Auckland Transport in the mid-2010s, and already investigated under the NZ Upgrade Programme.

contested.label: Projected full-corridor cost cited when the project was dropped
contested.note: What proceeding as originally scoped 'would have cost', per Michael Wood — a projection, not money spent. Never counted here.

contested.label: Projected cost of Stage 1 alone after the 2024 revival
contested.note: Future build cost for roughly a third of the corridor — close to the 2020 budget for the whole 21.5km. Not counted.

projects.summary: Funded 2020, scrapped 2021, revived 2024 — Stage 1 alone is now priced at nearly the whole 2020 budget.
projects.plain: A 21.5km corridor east of the Southern Motorway, from Manukau to south of Drury. Given $1.354b in the 2020 NZ Upgrade Programme, it was dropped in June 2021 after estimates ballooned to as much as $3.5b, then brought back as a Road of National Significance in 2024. Stage 1 construction was due to start as early as mid-2026 — six years after the road was first funded.

events.what: $1.354b allocated in the NZ Upgrade Programme for a 21.5km Manukau–Drury corridor.
Waka Kotahi takes over from Auckland Transport and continues buying properties along the corridor; spend undisclosed.
Dropped from the NZ Upgrade Programme after estimates hit up to $3.5b; replaced with safety improvements on the existing road plus SH1, rail and new-station investment around Drury.
Draft GPS 2024 revives Mill Road as a Road of National Significance.
Named among the 149 projects listed in the Fast-track Approvals Bill schedule.
NZTA board endorses the Stage 1 investment case and approves $91.1m for design and consents; construction as early as mid-2026.
RoNS progress update: Mill Road Stage 1 still working through its Fast-track Approvals Act application — consents not yet granted.

projects.name: Auckland Regional Fuel Tax
projects.firm_note: A tax repeal, not a project write-off: the ~$780m collected (to September 2023) was ring-fenced for legislated transport projects, and the unspent reserve stayed with three surviving priorities — so nothing is counted as sunk.

extra_costs.label: Reserve ring-fenced, projects descoped
extra_costs.note: ~$341m sat unspent as of September 2023 (MoT). From 8 March 2024 the reserve could legally fund only three projects — Eastern Busway, City Rail Link electric trains and stabling, and road corridor improvements — stripping the RFT funding stream from the other 11 legislated projects.

extra_costs.label: Scheme wind-down
extra_costs.note: NZTA estimated ~$3m would be needed over the two years after the scheme ended for rebate processing, compliance audits and administration, recovered from RFT revenue before transfer to Auckland Council (MoT briefing OC230866).

contested.label: Foregone RFT revenue to mid-2028 (MoT estimate)
contested.note: Officials' estimate of local revenue Auckland Council would lose from early termination (~$150m/year over four and a quarter years, calculated for a March 2024 end; the actual end was June 2024). Revenue never collected, not money spent — never counted.

contested.label: Auckland transport funding shortfall claimed by Mayor Wayne Brown
contested.note: Mayoral claim at repeal, bundling lost RFT revenue with the co-funding it leveraged. Attributed, not counted.

contested.label: Transport investment Auckland Council said was put at risk
contested.note: Council's framing of the total programme the RFT part-funded across 14 projects, recorded in MoT advice. A delivery-risk claim, not a cost.

projects.summary: Six years of 11.5c/L at the pump, axed four years early with ~$341m still unspent.
projects.plain: From July 2018 Aucklanders paid an extra 11.5 cents a litre to fund 14 transport projects, with the tax legislated to run until 2028. The incoming coalition repealed it under urgency and it ended on 30 June 2024 — by September 2023 about $780m had been collected but roughly $341m was still unspent. The remaining money was restricted to three projects, and the other eleven lost their funding stream.

events.what: Regional fuel tax legislation passes its third reading 63–57 — Labour, NZ First and the Greens in favour; National and ACT opposed.
10c/L plus GST (11.5c at the pump) takes effect across Auckland excluding Great Barrier Island, legislated to run to 30 June 2028 and raise ~$1.5b for 14 transport projects.

Transport Minister Simeon Brown confirms the tax will end 30 June 2024, fulfilling a coalition commitment, with repeal legislation to be introduced. ~$780m collected and ~$341m unspent as of September 2023.

Repeal bill completes its final stages under urgency on 5–6 March, skipping select committee — third reading 6 March, royal assent 7 March. From 8 March only the Eastern Busway, CRL electric trains and stabling, and road corridor improvements can draw on remaining funds.
Tax comes off at the pumps, four years before its legislated end; refund claims accepted until 31 October 2024.

projects.name: NZ Super Fund Contribution Suspension
projects.firm_note: A fiscal settings flip, not a project: nothing was built and nothing was written off. The only big number is the Guardians' counterfactual model of the compounding the Fund never did — a projection, so it lives in contested, not here.

contested.label: Guardians' modelled cost of the eight-year pause
contested.note: The Fund's own model, assessed at the December 2017 resumption: ~$12.5b of missed contributions, ~$12b of forgone returns on those contributions, and ~$3b of forgone domestic tax on those returns. The Guardians publish the three components, not a single total — the ~$27.5b is their sum. A counterfactual estimate, not money spent — and the flipside is the Crown borrowed less through the GFC. Never counted here.
contested.source: Guardians of NZ Super, contributions model page

projects.summary: Eight years of skipped payments; the Fund's own model prices the miss at ~$27.5b.
projects.plain: New Zealand saves into the Super Fund now so superannuation costs less later. National stopped the payments during the 2009 financial crisis and Labour–NZ First restarted them in December 2017. No money was written off, but the Fund's own modelling puts the cost of the eight-year pause at roughly $27.5 billion — $12.5b of missed contributions, $12b of returns those contributions never earned, and $3b of tax never paid on those returns.

events.what: The 'Cullen Fund' begins investing in October 2003 with a first contribution of $2.4b, under what is now the NZ Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001.

Budget 2009 suspends automatic contributions to avoid further debt; a final partial contribution of $250m goes in for 2009/10. Resumption waits on surpluses big enough to fund the formula — on Treasury's projections, 11 years away (about 2020/21).
Labour–NZ First resumes contributions — $7.7b over the next five years — with payments restarting the next day.
Robertson hits the button at Treasury on the first monthly instalment — $71m of the $500m planned for 2017/18 — with Ardern looking on. The first payment in nine years.
Contributions continue under the National-led coalition — this time the setting survives the change of government.
Budget 2025 diverts a further $61m of contributions to the Elevate NZ Venture Fund — on top of the $240m Labour–NZ First diverted to Elevate in 2019.
Budget 2026 lifts contributions: $3.1b forecast over the next four years, $2.2b more than previously signalled.

projects.name: RBNZ Dual Mandate
projects.firm_note: A statutory-settings flip: the employment objective was written into the Reserve Bank's mandate by agreement and statute, then struck out by statute. No identifiable Crown money was sunk on the reversed objective itself.
projects.summary: Employment written into the central bank's job in 2018, deleted under urgency in 2023 — the new government's first law.
projects.plain: In 2018 the Labour-led coalition gave the Reserve Bank two jobs: keep prices stable and support maximum sustainable employment. In December 2023 the incoming coalition repealed the employment half under urgency as the very first law it passed, returning the bank to a single price-stability target. Nothing was built or written off; the whiplash is in the rulebook the bank works to.

events.what: New Policy Targets Agreement signed by Grant Robertson and incoming Governor Adrian Orr adds 'maximum sustainable employment' alongside price stability.
Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Monetary Policy) Amendment Act 2018 receives royal assent, putting the dual mandate into statute.
Act fully in force: the new Monetary Policy Committee takes over under the dual-mandate remit, ending the Governor's sole responsibility for monetary policy.
Repeal listed in the coalition's 100-day plan: refocus the Reserve Bank on a single price-stability mandate.

Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill passes its third reading under urgency — the first legislation passed by the new government, taken through all stages in one extended sitting that began 12 December.
Royal assent on 19 December; new single-mandate remit takes effect the next day. Employment objective gone after five years.

projects.name: GIDI Decarbonisation Fund
projects.firm_note: A scheme termination with no exit write-off: grants already contracted were honoured and bought real boiler conversions, and the unspent balance was returned to the Crown, so nothing is counted as sunk.

extra_costs.label: Committed and honoured
extra_costs.note: Around 119 projects had roughly $355m of government co-funding committed, matched by over $890m in private funding (IEA/EECA); contracted projects continued after closure, including NZ Steel's part-funded electric arc furnace.

extra_costs.label: Clawed back
extra_costs.note: $640m of unspent GIDI funding was returned to government coffers after closure (RNZ, May 2024).

extra_costs.label: Aftermath
extra_costs.note: In October 2025 Cabinet redirected $4m of cancelled GIDI grant money toward procuring an LNG import terminal — half the $8m procurement budget (NZ Herald, Mar 2026).

contested.label: Treasury-estimated emissions savings foregone to 2050
contested.note: A projection of abatement the fund would have bought, not money spent. Never counted.

contested.label: ETS 'climate dividend' Willis said the closures freed for tax relief
contested.note: A forecast of future Emissions Trading Scheme cash proceeds across several programme closures, not GIDI-specific spending. Never counted.

projects.summary: Paid firms to ditch coal boilers; scrapped as 'corporate welfare' with $640m handed back.
projects.plain: A co-funding scheme that paid companies to swap coal and gas boilers for electric and biomass alternatives, launched in 2020 with $70m and expanded with roughly $650m more in 2022. The incoming coalition called it corporate welfare and scrapped it in the December 2023 mini-budget. About $640m of unspent funding went back to the government's books, while grants already contracted were honoured.

events.what: GIDI Fund launched by Ardern and Woods: $70m, administered by EECA, co-funding the switch from coal and gas boilers to electricity and biomass.
Budget 2022 'supercharges' GIDI with around $650m over four years from the Climate Emergency Response Fund.

Mini-budget closes GIDI — Willis: it 'has been subsidising already profitable businesses to reduce emissions'. Closure helps free $2.047b of forecast ETS proceeds as a 'climate dividend' for tax relief.
RNZ reports $640m of unspent GIDI funding returned to government coffers; Treasury estimated the fund would have delivered 10 Mt of CO₂ savings to 2050.
NZ Herald reveals Cabinet redirected $4m of cancelled GIDI grants to buy an LNG import terminal — half the $8m procurement budget.

projects.name: 90-day Trial Periods
projects.firm_note: A pure employment-law setting flip: no project to write off. The churn cost lands on employers and new hires re-papering employment agreements each time the threshold moves, not on the Crown.
projects.summary: Four settings in fifteen years: small firms, everyone, small firms, everyone.
projects.plain: A clause letting an employer dismiss a new hire in their first 90 days without facing an unjustified-dismissal claim. National introduced it for small employers in 2009 and extended it to everyone in 2011; Labour wound it back to small employers in 2019; the incoming coalition restored it to all employers within weeks of taking office in December 2023. Treasury-funded research found no evidence the trials increased overall hiring.

events.what: Introduced for employers with fewer than 20 employees (National, passed under urgency with royal assent 15 December 2008; trial-period sections in force 1 March 2009).
Extended to all employers (Employment Relations Amendment Act 2010, in force 1 April 2011).
Restricted back to employers with fewer than 20 employees (Labour's Employment Relations Amendment Act 2018, passed 6 December 2018).
Restored to all employers as a coalition 100-day-plan item; royal assent 22 December 2023, in force the next day.

projects.name: NZ Income Insurance Scheme

firm.label: ACC spend preparing to implement the scheme, then halting it — incl. $11.7m on contractors and consultants ($5.4m to PwC), ~$390k staff redundancies and $1.73m contractor termination costs
firm.source: NZ Herald (OIA figures from ACC), 5 May 2023

projects.firm_note: ACC's audited 2023 annual report independently corroborates the scale: ~$5m spent in 2021/22 plus $16.9m in 2022/23 before the programme was disestablished, with $19.6m of that year's $42.2m appropriation returned to the Crown. MBIE largely footed the bill for the policy design itself; that spend was never separately published and contributes $0 to totals here.

extra_costs.label: MBIE policy development
extra_costs.note: Two years of scheme design (2021-23) ran through MBIE and the tripartite forum with BusinessNZ and the NZCTU. No clean public figure for MBIE's share exists, so it is not counted.

contested.label: Estimated annual cost of the scheme once running, to be funded by new levies
contested.note: What the scheme would have cost to operate, paid by a 1.39% levy each on workers and employers. Never collected, never spent. Not counted.
contested.source: MBIE discussion document / NZ Herald, Feb 2022

projects.summary: Two years of tripartite design, an enabling act and a $21.6m ACC build-out — shelved by the government that designed it.
projects.plain: An ACC-style 'jobs insurance' scheme designed by the Labour government with BusinessNZ and the unions: lose your job to redundancy or ill health and you'd get 80% of your pay for up to seven months, funded by a new levy on workers and employers. ACC stood up a 30-person implementation unit under a 2022 enabling act, then Chris Hipkins shelved the whole thing in his February 2023 policy bonfire before the main legislation was ever introduced. ACC had spent $21.6m preparing for, and then unwinding, a scheme that never existed.

events.what: Budget 2021: Government, BusinessNZ and the CTU to jointly design an ACC-style social unemployment insurance scheme.
Tripartite discussion document released: 1.39% levy each on workers and employers, 80% of pay for up to seven months, run by ACC.
Enabling act received royal assent (third reading 20 May) so ACC could build delivery systems before the scheme itself was legislated — with a sunset clause if it never was.
Hipkins reprioritisation: income insurance 'off the table' — no scheme this term. ACC's implementation unit was subsequently disestablished and unspent funding returned to the Crown.
The enabling act self-repealed under its sunset clause. The scheme was never established.

projects.name: Road to Zero Speed Limit Reductions
projects.firm_note: Money was unquestionably spent twice — signs in, then signs out — but no clean nationwide actual is on the public record. Auckland Transport's $8.8m reversal figure is a board-paper forecast, the cost of the original reductions was never centrally totalled, and councils' spend on speed management plans voided by the 2024 rule is only patchily reported. Nothing is counted until an audited figure lands.

extra_costs.label: Scrapped speed management plans
extra_costs.note: The 2024 rule voided plans councils had not yet implemented. West Coast councils alone reported close to $500,000 sunk on their withdrawn draft plan — Buller $172,000, the regional council $78,000, Westland 'close to' Buller's figure, with the chair putting the combined total at 'pushing $500,000' (RNZ/LDR, Nov 2024).

extra_costs.label: Paying twice for signs
extra_costs.note: Councils installed lower-limit signs in 2020–23, then paid to take them down again. Auckland Transport's reversal programme covered 1,540 streets and 152 schools, unbudgeted in its regional transport plan, with NZTA paying 51% from the National Land Transport Fund.

extra_costs.label: Enforcement churn
extra_costs.note: NZTA cancelled and refunded 279 fines issued in a single day on a Lower Hutt street where successive changes left permanent and variable school-zone signs giving conflicting limits (RNZ, Mar 2026).

contested.label: Auckland Transport's forecast cost to reverse its speed limits
contested.note: A February 2025 board-paper estimate ('will likely cost'), down from an earlier $25m estimate ($7.5m signs and markings, $16.7m variable school limits, $450k advertising). A forecast, not confirmed spend — never counted.

contested.label: National's campaign ring-fence to fund reversals
contested.note: An 'initial' three-year allocation from the National Land Transport Fund, pledged in September 2023 to buy and install new signage and remove markings. An allocation, not reported spend.

projects.summary: Paid to put the signs up, paid to take them down.
projects.plain: Under Labour's Road to Zero strategy, NZTA and councils lowered speed limits on thousands of roads from 2020. The coalition's 2024 rule ordered limits lowered since January 2020 on specified roads back up by 1 July 2025, so the same stretches of road got new signs twice in five years. After consultation, a handful of roads kept their lower limits.

events.what: Road to Zero launched: cut road deaths and serious injuries 40% by 2030, with lower speed limits a key lever.
Setting of Speed Limits Rule 2022 takes effect: bylaws out, speed management plans in; reductions roll out across state highways and local roads.
National–ACT coalition agreement commits to 'reverse speed limit reductions where it is safe to do so'.
Setting of Speed Limits Rule 2024 signed: limits lowered since January 2020 on specified roads must revert by 1 July 2025; variable school-zone limits required by July 2026.
New rule takes effect, revoking the 2022 rule and voiding speed management plans councils had not yet implemented.
Reversals begin with SH2 Featherston–Masterton that night: 38 state highway sections auto-revert; 49 more go to six weeks of public consultation.
Consultation outcome: 43 of the 49 consulted state highway sections return to their previous higher limits; six keep their lower limits after clearing the 50% public-support threshold.
Deadline passes: specified roads nationwide back at their pre-2020 limits.
NZTA cancels and refunds 279 fines issued in a single day (16 November 2025) on Rata Street, Lower Hutt, where permanent and variable school-zone signs gave conflicting limits.

projects.name: East West Link
projects.firm_note: Stuff reported ~$50m spent by November 2017 (~$39m on consultation and consenting, ~$10m on early works including removing the old Onehunga rail bridge), but no primary NZTA figure for total spend on the original scheme is on the public record. Contributes $0 to every total here until one is sourced.

extra_costs.label: Revival re-planning
extra_costs.note: $102m approved in October 2025 to progress design, consenting and route protection for the scaled-back revival (Stage 1: Galway Link) — new money on the latest iteration, never counted as sunk (Beehive, 20 Oct 2025).

contested.note: Stuff reported ~$39m on the consultation and consenting process and ~$10m on early works. A single secondary report with no primary corroboration — never counted.

contested.note: NZTA's estimate at RMA lodgement; its per-km cost drew 'world's most expensive road per kilometre' headlines. What it would have cost, not what was spent.

contested.note: Roughly double the 2016 estimate. A projection, never counted.

projects.summary: Shelved 2017, consented 2018, overturned 2024, revived at double the price — no road yet.
projects.plain: A four-lane freight road between SH20 and SH1 through Auckland's Onehunga–Penrose industrial belt, first funded for investigation in 2014. Labour shelved the ~$1.85b design in late 2017 just before it won consent, and the Supreme Court overturned that consent in April 2024 — weeks after the new National-led government had revived the road. A scaled-back version got $102m for design and consenting in 2025; twelve years on, the road itself remains unbuilt.

events.what: $10m for East-West Link investigations in the National government's $375m accelerated Auckland transport package.
Notices of Requirement and consent applications lodged with the EPA; project estimated at $1.25b–$1.85b.
Incoming Labour-led government drops the project from its plans; Stuff reports ~$50m already spent on the now-'defunct' motorway.
Board of Inquiry confirms the designations and grants resource consents for the scheme the government had just shelved.
Twyford earmarks ~$800m for a lower-cost version via ATAP; it is never built either.
High Court dismisses appeals against the consents; Forest & Bird appeals on to the Supreme Court.
Draft GPS 2024 names the East West Link one of 15 Roads of National Significance.

Supreme Court allows Forest & Bird's appeal 4–1 on the result (William Young J dissenting; Glazebrook J concurring for different reasons), overturning the Board of Inquiry's approval and remitting the matter to it for reconsideration.
$102m approved for design, consenting and route protection of a scaled-back staged version; next steps include detailed design of Stage 1 (Galway Link).
NZTA aims to lodge statutory approvals for the redesigned corridor — largely avoiding the Māngere Inlet foreshore — in late 2026.
